title: ICE Body Camera Policy: Footage Released Only When in Agency's 'Best Interests'
excerpt: As ICE announced a nationwide body camera rollout by September 2026, reporting revealed the agency's written policy allows its director to withhold footage of shootings and other serious incidents unless releasing it is deemed to be in the "best interests of the agency."
content:
In early August 2026, after years of delays and amid mounting pressure following multiple fatal shootings of civilians by ICE agents, ICE announced that all field officers would be equipped with body-worn cameras by the end of September 2026 — pushed back from an earlier August 31 deadline.

However, reporting by the Associated Press, Boston Globe, and WBUR revealed that ICE's written body camera policy gives the agency director broad discretion over what footage the public can see. The policy states that ICE will promptly release video of shootings and other encounters in which agents cause death or serious injury only after determining "it is in the best interests of the agency" to do so — a standard criticized by body camera policy experts as enabling selective transparency.

  • ICE said cameras had been sent to more than half its field officers, with the remaining half to receive them by end of September.
  • At least one member of every arrest team would be required to have a camera, the agency said.
  • ICE officers in the Houston area — where the July 7 fatal shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo occurred without cameras — received more than 800 cameras as a priority.
  • Congress had provided $20 million specifically for body cameras and $31 billion more for broader technology, with no mandatory release requirement attached.
  • A DHS review committee would oversee decisions on releasing footage after serious incidents.
